title: A Distant backwater of the Milky Way
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6934, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6934 · constellation Delphinus · about 50000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A bright spray of stars fills this Hubble image of NGC 6934, a globular cluster in the small constellation Delphinus, the Dolphin. Globular clusters are big balls of ancient stars, usually a few hundred thousand of them, found on the outskirts of galaxies.

Lying 50 000 light-years away in the Milky Way's outer reaches, NGC 6934 holds some of the most distant stars still belonging to our galaxy. William Herschel first saw it in the late eighteenth century, but he could not resolve it into stars and classed it as a 'bright nebula'.

The cluster is invisible to the naked eye and very hard to see even with binoculars, yet amateur astronomers like it because fairly inexpensive telescopes show it easily. Its faintness comes from its distance, not a lack of stars, since it holds many thousands. Patrick Moore included it in his Caldwell catalog of objects for amateurs to seek out.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.33 x 3.33 arcminutes) and distance (50000 light years), the frame spans roughly 48 × 48 light-years. Its light set out about 50,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The near-infrared filter (F814W) is shown in red and the orange filter (F606W) in blue.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the cluster itself is too faint to see without a telescope.

explore: For more than 50 years Moore presented The Sky at Night on BBC TV. The picture was built from two filters, one near-infrared and one orange, with exposures of 29 minutes each, and it covers a field 3.3 arcminutes across.
alt: A bright spray of stars forming the globular cluster NGC 6934.
